stem: Why do random forests often generalize better than a single fully grown decision tree?

options.A: Averaging many decorrelated trees can reduce variance while retaining nonlinear interactions.
options.C: Every tree receives exactly the same features and bootstrap sample.
options.D: A random forest is always linear in the original features.

rationales.correct: Bagging reduces variance by averaging unstable base learners, while feature subsampling helps decorrelate trees. The result can be much more stable than one high-variance tree.
rationales.B: Ensembling can retain bias; it is not a universal bias eliminator.
rationales.C: Randomization is used specifically to diversify trees.

stem: In gradient boosting, what is the high-level role of each successive weak learner?

options.A: It is trained to reduce current model error, commonly by fitting the negative gradient/residual structure of the current loss.
options.B: It independently replaces the entire ensemble.
options.C: It is trained only on the original unmodified labels with no relationship to the current model.
options.D: It randomly permutes the target to reduce variance.

rationales.correct: Boosting constructs an additive model sequentially. Each learner is chosen to improve the current ensemble, often by approximating a gradient direction of the loss.
rationales.B: The learner contributes an incremental function to the ensemble.
rationales.C: Its training target is derived from the current model and chosen loss, directly or indirectly.
rationales.D: Target permutation would destroy the learning signal.

stem: A boosted-tree model overfits after hundreds of stages. Which change directly reduces ensemble complexity while preserving the sequential boosting idea?

options.A: Reduce the number of boosting stages, decrease tree depth, increase regularization, or use a smaller learning rate with appropriate early stopping.
options.B: Increase the number of stages without validation monitoring.

rationales.correct: Boosting has several complexity controls: number/depth of base learners, shrinkage, subsampling, and regularization. Early stopping can select an appropriate number of stages.
rationales.D: Validation monitoring is useful for detecting the point at which generalization degrades.

stem: Why are decision trees generally less sensitive to monotonic feature scaling than distance-based algorithms such as k-NN?

options.A: A standard decision tree chooses threshold splits based on ordering; multiplying a feature by a positive constant preserves that ordering with transformed thresholds.
options.D: Scaling converts a tree into a linear model.

rationales.correct: For a strictly monotonic rescaling such as multiplication by a positive constant, the ranking/order of feature values is preserved, so equivalent threshold partitions remain available.
rationales.B: Trees can use numeric features directly.
rationales.C: Distance computation is not how ordinary axis-aligned tree splits are selected.
rationales.D: Scaling does not change tree models into linear models.

stem: What is the key idea behind the kernel trick in an SVM?

options.A: Compute inner products in an implicit feature space using a kernel function without explicitly constructing all transformed coordinates.
options.B: Replace the training labels with kernel values.
options.C: Guarantee that every kernelized classifier is linear in the original input space.
options.D: Avoid all computational cost associated with pairwise similarities.

rationales.correct: A valid positive-semidefinite kernel can represent inner products in a feature space. Algorithms such as kernel SVMs can work through kernel evaluations rather than explicitly materializing the mapping.
rationales.B: Kernels operate on input pairs, not label replacement.
rationales.C: The classifier is linear in feature space but can be nonlinear in the original input space.
rationales.D: Kernel methods may require many pairwise kernel evaluations and can become computationally costly.

stem: For an RBF-kernel SVM, increasing gamma while keeping C fixed generally makes the kernel similarity decay more rapidly with distance. What is the likely modeling effect?

options.A: The decision boundary can become more local and flexible, increasing the risk of fitting fine-grained structure or noise.
options.B: The model is forced to become a straight line.
options.C: All training points become equally similar.
options.D: The number of support vectors must become exactly zero.

rationales.correct: For the RBF kernel K(x,x') = exp(-gamma ||x-x'||²), larger gamma creates narrower similarity neighborhoods, allowing more localized decision structure.
rationales.B: A larger gamma generally increases flexibility rather than enforcing linearity.
rationales.C: Similarity becomes more localized, not uniform.
rationales.D: Support-vector count depends on the data, C, gamma, and optimization outcome.

stem: In a soft-margin SVM, what is the conceptual role of C?

options.A: It controls the tradeoff between a wider margin and penalties for violating the margin or misclassifying training examples.
options.B: It directly sets the number of classes.
options.C: It is the RBF gamma parameter.
options.D: It forces all support vectors to disappear.

rationales.correct: The soft-margin formulation balances margin size against slack/violation penalties. Larger C penalizes violations more heavily, usually permitting a narrower margin to fit training data more aggressively.
rationales.B: C is not a class-count parameter.
rationales.C: Gamma controls kernel width/locality for kernels such as RBF; it is a different hyperparameter.
rationales.D: Support vectors generally remain part of the solution.

stem: A random forest has 500 trees and the validation prediction hardly changes when increasing to 700 trees. What is the most reasonable interpretation?

options.A: The ensemble may already have reached a point of diminishing variance reduction; more trees can stabilize estimates but may add little predictive gain.
options.B: The forest has become underfit because too many trees always increase bias.
options.C: The extra trees must be using test-set information.
options.D: Random forests stop working after 500 trees by definition.

rationales.correct: As the number of sufficiently diverse trees increases, averaging can approach a stable prediction; extra trees often yield diminishing returns rather than a guaranteed accuracy jump.
rationales.B: Adding trees to a fixed random-forest design is not generally a monotonic bias-increasing operation.
rationales.C: No test leakage follows from the tree count itself.
